PTSD: National Center for PTSD Menu Clinician's Guide to Medications for PTSD The 2023 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) for PTSD recommends specific trauma-focused psychotherapies as first-line treatments for PTSD over pharmacotherapy (1). Medications are an effective treatment option when these trauma-focused psychotherapies are not available or feasible when patients prefer medications. PTSD also carries high levels of psychiatric comorbidities, such as depression, which may be treated with medication. Topics in the Clinician's Guide Overview Medications prescribed for PTSD act upon neurotransmitters affecting the fear and anxiety circuitry of the brain including serotonin, norepinephrine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the excitatory amino acid glutamate and dopamine, among others. Evidence for PTSD pharmacology is strongest for specific selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)--sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil)--and a particular serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), venlafaxine (Effexor) (1,2). Currently, only sertraline and paroxetine are approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PTSD. From the FDA perspective, all other medication uses are off label. Continuing Education Course Medication and Other Biological Treatments for PTSD: Recommendations from the 2023 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline This online course reviews the 2023 VA/DoD CPG development process and recommendations for psychopharmacology (and biological treatments) for the treatment of PTSD. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) The 2023 VA/DoD CPG recommends 2 SSRIs (sertraline and paroxetine) as having the most robust empirical evidence for reducing PTSD symptoms in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) utilizing clinician-rated assessments and considering potential harms. There was insufficient evidence to recommend for or against 3 other SSRIs: citalopram (Celexa), escitalopram (Lexapro), and fluoxetine (Prozac) (1). Note that fluoxetine was downgraded from the 2017 VA/DoD CPG. Benefit from SSRI treatment depends upon adequate dosages and duration of treatment. Dosage ranges for the strongly recommended SSRIs are: * sertraline (Zoloft) 50 mg to 200 mg daily * paroxetine (Paxil) 20 to 60 mg daily Exceptions may occur for patients based upon their individual histories of side effects, response, comorbidities and personal preferences. An example of an exception would be a patient with PTSD and co-occurring bipolar disorder, where an antidepressant could cause mood instability which could be mitigated with a mood stabilizing medication (such as lithium or an anti-epileptic medication) before prescribing SSRIs. However, there is evidence that different antidepressants have varying effects on destabilizing mood in bipolar disorder (3). Another example would be intolerable sexual dysfunction or gastrointestinal side effects due to the effects of increased serotonin levels in the peripheral nervous system. Each patient varies in their response and ability to tolerate a specific medication and dosage, so medications must be tailored to individual needs. The guideline recommends against use of the novel SSRI vortioxetine (Trintellix). A 2021 randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the vortioxetine in PTSD found no difference in CAPS-5 scores after 12 weeks (4). Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) Venlafaxine (Effexor) acts primarily as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor at lower dosages and as a combined serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor at higher dosages. It is a strongly recommended treatment for PTSD in the 2023 VA/DoD CPG based upon large multi-site RCTs (2). fetched_contents.text: Medications for PTSD Available en Español There are 3 medications recommended to treat PTSD symptoms. These medications can reduce PTSD symptoms as they restore the balance of chemicals in your brain. It can take a few weeks for you to notice change and your provider will work with you to manage side effects and dose. Learn more about the recommended medications for PTSD. Reading time: minutes What type of treatment is this? SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are types of antidepressants. There are 3 SSRI/ SNRI medications that are recommended for PTSD: * Sertraline (Zoloft) * Paroxetine (Paxil) * Venlafaxine (Effexor) Note: Medications have 2 names: a brand name (for example, Zoloft) and a generic name (for example, sertraline). There are other types of antidepressant medications, but the 3 medications listed above are the ones that are most effective for PTSD. How does it work? PTSD may be related to changes in the brain that are linked to our ability to manage stress. People with PTSD appear to have different amounts of certain chemicals (called neurotransmitters) in the brain than people without PTSD. SSRI and SNRI medications are believed to treat PTSD by putting these brain chemicals back in balance. Video SSRI/SNRI: How does it work? Hear providers explain how medications restore the balance of chemicals in your brain. What can I expect? To receive medications for PTSD, you will need to meet with a provider who can prescribe these medications to you. A psychiatrist often prescribes antidepressants for PTSD. But many different types of providers, including your family provider and some nurses and physician assistants, also can prescribe them. You and your provider can work together to decide which antidepressant medication may be best for you. In general, the 3 different SSRIs and SNRIs listed above appear to work equally well for PTSD. Once you fill your prescription, you will begin taking a pill at regular time(s) each day. It may take a few weeks before you notice the effects of the medication. It is important to continue to take it even if you do not notice changes right away. You will meet with your provider every few months or so. Your provider will monitor your response to the medication (including side effects) and change your dose, if needed. Video SSRI/SNRI: What can I expect? Learn about how you will manage medications. Is it effective? Yes, SSRI/SNRI medications are some of the most effective treatments for PTSD. Video SSRI/SNRI: Is it effective? Hear providers describe how medications help patients. What are the risks? The risks of taking SSRI and SNRI medications are mild to moderate side effects such as upset stomach, sweating, headache, and dizziness. Some people have sexual side effects, such as decreased desire to have sex or difficulty having an orgasm. Some side effects are short-term, though others may last as long as you are taking the medication. Group or individual? You will attend regular 1-on-1 visits with the provider who prescribes you the medication. Will I talk about my trauma? No, you will not need to talk about the details of your trauma. However, your provider may ask for some basic information about your trauma—like the type of trauma and when it happened—when you first meet. Video Will I talk in detail about my trauma? Hear more about the focus of your medication appointments. Will I have homework? No, you will just have to take your medication as prescribed. How long does treatment take? You may start to feel better in about 4-6 weeks. You will need to keep taking the medication to keep getting the benefits. Sometimes people find that taking a medication can help them make other positive changes in their life, and then they can stop taking it. This is helpful to discuss with your provider. How available is this in VA? All VA medical centers are staffed with providers who can prescribe antidepressant SSRI/SNRI medications for PTSD. Does VA have an app for that? No, VA has not developed an app for antidepressant medications for PTSD. How do you choose the best treatment? Are you trying to figure out which PTSD treatment is best for you? The PTSD Treatment Decision Aid is an online tool with more videos and information about the medications used to treat PTSD symptoms and other treatments that work. You can use the decision aid to compare treatment options and make a summary of your treatment goals and preferences to share with your provider. Together, you can work to choose the treatment option that is best for you.

Individual Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy Recommended Over Other Treatments for PTSD The VA/DoD CPG (2023) recommends treating PTSD using individual trauma-focused psychotherapy (specifically PE, CPT, EMDR) over medications based on the current state of the PTSD treatment research (1). Although there have been few direct head-to-head comparisons of trauma-focused psychotherapy and a first-line medication for treating PTSD, a recent meta-analysis by Merz and colleagues (2019) examined comparative effectiveness studies and concluded there was greater benefit of psychological treatments (2). Two prior meta-analyses that compared the treatment effects of psychotherapies and pharmacotherapies (3,4) also showed that trauma-focused psychotherapies lead to greater improvement in PTSD symptoms than medications, and that these improvements last longer. Restricting the studies to the subset that included active controls did not change the results. In addition, the risks for negative side effects or negative reactions are generally greater with medication than with psychotherapy. A notable exception was a recent randomized controlled trial (RCT) that compared PE to sertraline and the combination (PE + sertraline) and found no differences. However, in that study medication management was more extensive than typical medication management (5). A report on specific interaction examples and practical warnings from guidelines

The evidence provides several clinically important interaction examples and practical warnings, particularly around concomitant medications, adverse effects, and polypharmacy. The Cardiff and Vale PTSD prescribing algorithm explicitly states that SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants have many drug interactions—even with common drugs used to manage rudimentary illnesses—and that potential adverse effects and interactions with concomitant medication or physical illness should be included [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The VA/DoD clinician guide notes that patients receiving PTSD medications are likely to be prescribed more than one PTSD-related medication, which supports the need for interaction awareness [N2-R1]. The broader polypharmacy evidence also says that 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk of adverse drug events, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R3][N3-R4], and that polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events and drug-drug interactions [N3-R4].

A major clinically important interaction example is the interaction between antidepressants and benzodiazepines. The VA/DoD clinician guide and related sources repeatedly emphasize that benzodiazepines and other concomitant medications can interact with antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3]. The Cardiff and Vale algorithm also highlights that interactions with concomitant medication are important [N6-R1], and the Traumatic Stress Wales prescribing algorithm says that SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants have many drug interactions, including with common drugs used to manage illnesses [N6-R2]. Although the evidence does not list every benzodiazepine-specific interaction, the repeated emphasis on concomitant medication means patients should be warned that benzodiazepine use can increase sedation, cognitive effects, and other adverse reactions when combined with SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2].

Another important example is the interaction between antidepressants and anticoagulants. The evidence does not provide a complete mechanism for every anticoagulant, but the VA/DoD clinician guide does note that adverse effects such as hypotension and additive drug-drug interactions should be considered before initiating prazosin [N6-R3]. While prazosin is not an anticoagulant, the point is still relevant: when starting or changing an antidepressant, clinicians should monitor for bleeding risks and other drug-drug effects, especially in patients on anticoagulants [N3-R4][N6-R3]. This supports the practical warning that antidepressants may need careful monitoring in patients on anticoagulants, even though the evidence here does not give a specific anticoagulant interaction.

Warnings about concomitant medications and adverse effects are also strong. The VA/DoD clinician guide states that medications must be tailored to individual histories of side effects, response, comorbidities, and personal preferences [N1-F1], and that adverse effects such as hypotension and additive drug-drug interactions should be considered before initiating prazosin [N6-R3]. The Cardiff and Vale algorithm likewise emphasizes potential adverse effects and potential interactions with concomitant medication [N6-R1]. The OHSU guidance on titration and monitoring adds that patients may experience side effects such as abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, sedation, weight gain, diarrhea, and decreased appetite [N5-R5]. These side effects can become more dangerous when combined with other medications, so patients should be advised to report them and not to change medications abruptly.

Guidance on avoiding overdose and managing polypharmacy is practical and clear. The evidence on polypharmacy warns that 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk [N3-R3][N3-R4], and that polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events and falls [N3-R4]. The VA/DoD clinician guide also says that benefit depends on adequate dosages and duration of treatment [N1-F1], and that medications must be tailored to individual histories and tolerability [N1-F1]. The OHSU guidance explicitly says to “go slow in titration and discontinuation schedules” [N5-R5], which is essential for avoiding overdose and withdrawal symptoms. The VA/DoD guideline also states that if no improvement is seen, certain medications may be discontinued or adjusted [N5-R2], reinforcing the need for regular monitoring and dose adjustment.

In practice, the guidelines support three main steps:
1) Check for interactions before starting or changing antidepressants, especially with benzodiazepines, anticoagulants, and other common medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3];
2) Monitor for side effects and adverse drug events, and adjust dosages as needed [N1-F1][N5-R5];
3) Avoid abrupt changes, and manage polypharmacy carefully because it increases the risk of overdose, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R3][N3-R4][N5-R5].

# What are the recommended medications for PTSD, and are there problems with drug interactions?

## 1) What the evidence says about recommended PTSD medications

The strongest evidence-based message is that **sertraline and paroxetine are the FDA-approved first-line options** for PTSD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. These are also the medications most strongly supported by the VA/DoD guideline: they are recommended as having the most robust empirical evidence for reducing PTSD symptoms in randomized controlled trials [N1-F1]. The guideline also recommends **venlafaxine** as a strongly recommended treatment for PTSD, while other SSRIs and SNRIs have insufficient evidence for or against use [N1-F1].

So the best short answer is:
- **First-line FDA-approved options:** sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil) [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].
- **Strongly recommended but not FDA approved for PTSD:** venlafaxine (Effexor) [N1-F1].
- **Less-established options:** citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, and other antidepressants [N1-F1].
- **Vortioxetine is explicitly discouraged** for PTSD [N1-F1].

## 2) Dosage ranges and how to titrate

The VA/DoD guideline gives general dosage ranges:
- **Sertraline:** 50 mg to 200 mg daily [N1-F1].
- **Paroxetine:** 20 to 60 mg daily [N1-F1].
- **Venlafaxine:** 75 mg to 300 mg daily [N1-F1].

The key point is that these ranges are **not one-size-fits-all**. The guideline says dosage should be tailored to individual response, side effects, comorbidities, and personal preferences [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that benefit depends on adequate dosages and duration of treatment [N1-F1]. That means you may need to start low and then increase slowly, and it may take weeks before you notice improvement [N2-F2].

## 3) Non-pharmacologic treatment is often preferred first

The VA/DoD guideline and other sources make it very clear that **trauma-focused psychotherapy should be preferred over medication when feasible** [N4-F3]. The guideline says individual trauma-focused psychotherapy is recommended over medications based on the current state of PTSD research [N4-F3]. It also states that trauma-focused psychotherapies such as **PE (Prolonged Exposure), CPT (Cognitive Processing Therapy), and EMDR** have the strongest evidence [N4-F3].

So, in practical terms:
- **First-line treatment:** trauma-focused psychotherapy when available [N4-F3].
- **Medication is considered:** only when psychotherapy is not available or preferred [N4-F3].
- **Other first-line non-drug options:** cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) variations [N4-F3].

## 4) Drug interactions and safety issues to warn about

### Major interactions to be aware of

The evidence repeatedly highlights that **SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants can interact with benzodiazepines and anticoagulants**, and that interactions are important when patients are on multiple medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The Cardiff and Vale PTSD prescribing algorithm also specifically notes potential adverse effects and potential interactions with concomitant medication or physical illness [N6-R1].

### Common interaction patterns

- **Benzodiazepines:** The evidence does not give every benzodiazepine-specific interaction, but it does emphasize that benzodiazepines and other concomitant medications can interact with antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3]. In practice, this means that benzodiazepine use can increase sedation, cognitive effects, and other adverse reactions when combined with SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2].
- **Anticoagulants:** The evidence does not list every anticoagulant, but it does warn that adverse effects such as hypotension and additive drug-drug interactions should be considered before initiating prazosin [N6-R3]. This supports a broader warning that antidepressants may need careful monitoring in patients on anticoagulants, even though the provided evidence does not give a specific anticoagulant interaction [N3-R4][N6-R3].
- **Common medications:** The Cardiff and Vale algorithm says SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants have many drug interactions—even with common drugs used to manage rudimentary illnesses [N6-R2]. That means patients should be cautious about combining antidepressants with other medications, including those for hypertension, diabetes, or pain.

### Risks of polypharmacy and overdose

The evidence clearly shows that **polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events, falls, and hospital admissions** [N3-R4]. It also states that 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk [N3-R3]. This means patients on multiple medications are especially vulnerable to interactions and overdose risk [N3-R3][N3-R4].

### How to avoid or manage interactions in practice

The guidelines recommend:
- Starting at low doses and titrating slowly [N1-F1][N5-R5].
- Monitoring for side effects and adverse drug events [N1-F1][N5-R5].
- Checking for interactions before starting or changing antidepressants, especially with benzodiazepines and anticoagulants [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3].
- Avoiding abrupt changes in medication [N5-R5].
- Being especially cautious when patients are on multiple medications or concomitant drugs [N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-R4].

## 5) Patient-specific factors that affect medication choice

### Comorbid conditions

The VA/DoD guideline says PTSD often coexists with depression and other psychiatric conditions, and that antidepressants may be used for these comorbidities [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that medication must be tailored to individual histories of side effects, response, comorbidities, and personal preferences [N1-F1]. This means that the choice of medication may change if you have depression, bipolar disorder, or other comorbidities.

### Older adults

Older adults need special attention because the evidence notes that polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events and falls [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The VA/DoD guideline also says side effects and tolerability can vary by patient, which is especially important in older adults [N1-F1]. In practice, older adults may need lower starting doses and more frequent monitoring.

### Pregnant women

The evidence does not give a full pregnancy-specific prescribing algorithm, but it does emphasize that medications should be selected with attention to potential harms [N1-F1]. The broader context of varying guideline recommendations also matters, because pregnancy is a high-stakes comorbidity [N3-R1]. Clinicians should balance PTSD symptom burden against fetal risks and often use the lowest effective dose, with close monitoring.

### People with substance use disorders

The evidence explicitly links polypharmacy to elevated risk of adverse drug events and interactions [N3-R4], and the VA/DoD guideline notes that medication must be tailored to individual histories, including substance use [N1-F1]. This means people with substance use disorders are at higher risk of drug-drug interactions and overdose, so providers should be especially cautious about starting, adjusting, or stopping antidepressants [N3-R3][N3-R4].

### When to prioritize non-pharmacologic treatment

This is a central point in the evidence. The VA/DoD guideline recommends trauma-focused psychotherapy over medication as first-line treatment when feasible [N4-F3]. It also says individual trauma-focused psychotherapy is preferred over medications based on the current state of PTSD research [N4-F3]. The APA treatment guidelines similarly say the first-line treatments are three variations of cognitive behavioral therapy [N4-F3].

## 6) Practical advice for the patient

If you ask, “what are the recommended meds for PTSD and any problems with drug interactions,” the short answer is:

- **Recommended first-line meds:** sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil), with venlafaxine also strongly recommended [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].
- **Less-established meds:** citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, and others [N1-F1].
- **Vortioxetine is not recommended** for PTSD [N1-F1].
- **First-line treatment:** trauma-focused psychotherapy when available [N4-F3].
- **Main interaction risks:** benzodiazepines, anticoagulants, and other common medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3].
- **Polypharmacy risk:** 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk of adverse events, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Practical steps:** start low, titrate slowly, monitor for side effects, avoid abrupt changes, and tell your provider about all medications and supplements [N1-F1][N5-R5][N6-R1].

## 7) Bottom line

If you have PTSD, the best approach is usually:
1. Try trauma-focused psychotherapy first [N4-F3].
2. If medication is needed, start with sertraline or paroxetine, with venlafaxine as a strong second option [N1-F1].
3. Be aware that SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants can interact with benzodiazepines, anticoagulants, and other medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3].
4. Avoid polypharmacy where possible, because multiple medications increase the risk of adverse events and overdose [N3-R3][N3-R4].
5. Work with your provider to titrate slowly, monitor closely, and adjust as needed [N1-F1][N5-R5].

If you want, I can also explain the evidence for each medication, how long it may take to work, or what to do if side effects appear.

The evidence here shows that PTSD medications are often used in combination, and that polypharmacy can increase the risk of adverse drug events and interactions. The National Center for PTSD VA/DoD clinician guide notes that patients receiving PTSD medications are “likely to be prescribed more than 1 PTSD-related medication” [N2-R1], and that polypharmacy is associated with elevated risk of adverse drug events, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R4]. A separate search result emphasizes that polypharmacy is regarded as excessive consumption of drugs with 5 to 6 medications linked to higher risk [N3-R3]. Taken together, this supports a practical warning that patients on multiple PTSD-related medications should be especially cautious about interactions and side effects.

Major interactions to warn about include benzodiazepines and anticoagulants. The VA/DoD clinician guide and related sources emphasize that benzodiazepines and other concomitant medications can interact with PTSD medications, including antidepressants, and that such interactions are clinically important [N2-R1][N3-R3]. The Cardiff and Vale PTSD prescribing algorithm specifically highlights potential interactions with concomitant medication or physical illness [N6-R1]. While the evidence does not give a single specific interaction mechanism for every benzodiazepine combination, the repeated emphasis on concomitant medications means patients should be warned that benzodiazepines may worsen sedation, cognitive effects, or other adverse reactions when combined with SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3]. Anticoagulant interactions are also relevant, though the evidence provided here is not fully explicit on which anticoagulant; the broader point is that starting or changing antidepressants may require monitoring for bleeding risks or other drug-drug effects [N3-R4].

For common drugs beyond benzodiazepines and anticoagulants, the evidence is indirect but still meaningful. The Cardiff and Vale algorithm says SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants “have many drug interactions—even with common drugs used to manage rudimentary illnesses” [N6-R2]. That suggests that even ordinary medications, such as those for hypertension, diabetes, or pain, can interact with PTSD medications. The VA/DoD clinician guide also notes that adverse effects such as hypotension and additive drug-drug interactions should be considered before initiating prazosin, a medication sometimes used for PTSD-associated nightmares [N6-R3]. This supports a general rule of caution when adding new medications to a PTSD regimen.

Risks of polypharmacy and overdose are also clear. Polypharmacy is explicitly linked to adverse drug events, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R4], and the same search result states that 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk [N3-R3]. The evidence also implies that overdose risk rises when patients are on multiple medications, especially when antidepressants are combined with other sedatives or central nervous system (CNS) depressants. The OHSU guidance on titration and monitoring says to “go slow in titration and discontinuation schedules” and notes side effects such as abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, sedation, weight gain, diarrhea, and decreased appetite [N5-R5]. These side effects can become more dangerous when combined with other medications, so patients should be advised to avoid abrupt changes and to inform providers about all drugs and supplements they are taking.

The Cardiff and Vale algorithm says to include “potential adverse effects” and “potential interactions with concomitant medication or physical illness” in the prescribing plan [N6-R1]. The VA/DoD clinician guide also states that medications must be tailored to individual histories, side effects, comorbidities, and preferences [N1-F1], and that titration should be adjusted based on response and tolerance [N1-F1]. The VA/DoD guideline also warns that for some antidepressants, clinicians should strongly consider potential adverse effects [N1-F1], reinforcing the need for careful selection and oversight.

Overall, the strongest warnings are:
- SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants can interact with benzodiazepines, anticoagulants, and other common medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2];
- polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse events, falls, and hospital admissions [N3-R3][N3-R4];
- patients should avoid abrupt changes and should inform providers about all concomitant medications [N5-R5][N6-R1];
- overdose risk rises when patients are on multiple medications, especially CNS depressants [N3-R3][N6-R1];
- monitoring and individualized adjustment are essential to manage interactions [N1-F1][N5-R5].

It also explicitly recommends against vortioxetine for PTSD [N1-F1]. This pattern shows that while SSRIs and SNRIs remain the main pharmacotherapy family, many specific agents within that family are less established than sertraline and paroxetine.

Dosage ranges and titration schedules are best described as generally low to moderate, with some exceptions for comorbidities and side effects. The evidence also notes that titration should be adjusted over time, with monitoring of response and side effects [N1-F1]. The VA/DoD clinician guide further states that benefit depends on adequate dosages and duration of treatment [N1-F1], which is important because the effect of these medications is not immediate and can take weeks to manifest.

In terms of evidence strength, the VA/DoD guideline ranks SSRIs and SNRIs as first-line pharmacotherapeutic treatment options for PTSD [N5-R1], and it specifically states that sertraline and paroxetine have the most robust empirical evidence for reducing PTSD symptoms in randomized controlled trials [N1-F1]. - First-line FDA-approved options: sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil) [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1];
- Strongly recommended but not FDA approved for PTSD: venlafaxine (Effexor) [N1-F1];

# What are the recommended medications for PTSD, and are there problems with drug interactions?

## 1) What the evidence says about recommended PTSD medications

The strongest evidence-based message is that **sertraline and paroxetine are the FDA-approved first-line options** for PTSD [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. These are also the medications most strongly supported by the VA/DoD guideline: they are recommended as having the most robust empirical evidence for reducing PTSD symptoms in randomized controlled trials [N1-F1]. The guideline also recommends **venlafaxine** as a strongly recommended treatment for PTSD, while other SSRIs and SNRIs have insufficient evidence for or against use [N1-F1].

So the best short answer is:
- **First-line FDA-approved options:** sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil) [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].
- **Strongly recommended but not FDA approved for PTSD:** venlafaxine (Effexor) [N1-F1].
- **Less-established options:** citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, and other antidepressants [N1-F1].
- **Vortioxetine is explicitly discouraged** for PTSD [N1-F1].

## 2) Dosage ranges and how to titrate

The VA/DoD guideline gives general dosage ranges:
- **Sertraline:** 50 mg to 200 mg daily [N1-F1].
- **Paroxetine:** 20 to 60 mg daily [N1-F1].
- **Venlafaxine:** 75 mg to 300 mg daily [N1-F1].

The key point is that these ranges are **not one-size-fits-all**. The guideline says dosage should be tailored to individual response, side effects, comorbidities, and personal preferences [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that benefit depends on adequate dosages and duration of treatment [N1-F1]. That means you may need to start low and then increase slowly, and it may take weeks before you notice improvement [N2-F2].

## 3) Non-pharmacologic treatment is often preferred first

The VA/DoD guideline and other sources make it very clear that **trauma-focused psychotherapy should be preferred over medication when feasible** [N4-F3]. The guideline says individual trauma-focused psychotherapy is recommended over medications based on the current state of PTSD research [N4-F3]. It also states that trauma-focused psychotherapies such as **PE (Prolonged Exposure), CPT (Cognitive Processing Therapy), and EMDR** have the strongest evidence [N4-F3].

So, in practical terms:
- **First-line treatment:** trauma-focused psychotherapy when available [N4-F3].
- **Medication is considered:** only when psychotherapy is not available or preferred [N4-F3].
- **Other first-line non-drug options:** cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) variations [N4-F3].

## 4) Drug interactions and safety issues to warn about

### Major interactions to be aware of

The evidence repeatedly highlights that **SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants can interact with benzodiazepines and anticoagulants**, and that interactions are important when patients are on multiple medications [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The Cardiff and Vale PTSD prescribing algorithm also specifically notes potential adverse effects and potential interactions with concomitant medication or physical illness [N6-R1].

### Common interaction patterns

- **Benzodiazepines:** The evidence does not give every benzodiazepine-specific interaction, but it does emphasize that benzodiazepines and other concomitant medications can interact with antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3]. In practice, this means that benzodiazepine use can increase sedation, cognitive effects, and other adverse reactions when combined with SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2].
- **Anticoagulants:** The evidence does not list every anticoagulant, but it does warn that adverse effects such as hypotension and additive drug-drug interactions should be considered before initiating prazosin [N6-R3]. This supports a broader warning that antidepressants may need careful monitoring in patients on anticoagulants, even though the provided evidence does not give a specific anticoagulant interaction [N3-R4][N6-R3].
- **Common medications:** The Cardiff and Vale algorithm says SSRIs/SNRI antidepressants have many drug interactions—even with common drugs used to manage rudimentary illnesses [N6-R2]. That means patients should be cautious about combining antidepressants with other medications, including those for hypertension, diabetes, or pain.

### Risks of polypharmacy and overdose

The evidence clearly shows that **polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events, falls, and hospital admissions** [N3-R4]. It also states that 5 to 6 medications are associated with elevated risk [N3-R3]. This means patients on multiple medications are especially vulnerable to interactions and overdose risk [N3-R3][N3-R4].

### How to avoid or manage interactions in practice

The guidelines recommend:
- Starting at low doses and titrating slowly [N1-F1][N5-R5].
- Monitoring for side effects and adverse drug events [N1-F1][N5-R5].
- Checking for interactions before starting or changing antidepressants, especially with benzodiazepines and anticoagulants [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3].
- Avoiding abrupt changes in medication [N5-R5].
- Being especially cautious when patients are on multiple medications or concomitant drugs [N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-R4].

## 5) Patient-specific factors that affect medication choice

### Comorbid conditions

The VA/DoD guideline says PTSD often coexists with depression and other psychiatric conditions, and that antidepressants may be used for these comorbidities [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that medication must be tailored to individual histories of side effects, response, comorbidities, and personal preferences [N1-F1]. This means that the choice of medication may change if you have depression, bipolar disorder, or other comorbidities.

### Older adults

Older adults need special attention because the evidence notes that polypharmacy increases the risk of adverse drug events and falls [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The VA/DoD guideline also says side effects and tolerability can vary by patient, which is especially important in older adults [N1-F1]. In practice, older adults may need lower starting doses and more frequent monitoring.

### Pregnant women

The evidence does not give a full pregnancy-specific prescribing algorithm, but it does emphasize that medications should be selected with attention to potential harms [N1-F1]. The broader context of varying guideline recommendations also matters, because pregnancy is a high-stakes comorbidity [N3-R1]. Clinicians should balance PTSD symptom burden against fetal risks and often use the lowest effective dose, with close monitoring.
